### 7.2.4 Civil Law Doctrine, the EU AI Act, and Personal Data Protection

When mental autonomy is systematically engineered and destroyed by algorithms, how does the legal system respond? Are existing civil law principles and data‑protection regulations sufficient to provide a remedy for victims of algorithmic manipulation? To answer this question, we must scrutinize the prevailing positive civil law doctrine—particularly the requirements for a valid contract and defects of will—alongside modern legislative instruments such as the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022).

Within the conventional civil‑law framework, Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) stipulates that one of the essential elements of a valid contract is the “mutual agreement of the parties who bind themselves” (Subekti, 2005). Moreover, Article 1321 Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) declares that an agreement is void if consent is given because of a mistake (*dwaling*), coercion (*dwang*), or fraud (*bedrog*) (Salim HS, 2008). For centuries, this doctrine has been understood in the context of interpersonal interactions among physically and cognitively equal agents. Yet how should we apply it when a digital transaction or consent—such as an extensive, manipulative terms‑of‑service agreement or an impulsive purchase driven by AI‑powered dark patterns—is preceded by behavioral engineering that systematically impairs an individual’s cognitive capacities? (Hildebrandt, 2015; Farahany, 2023).

```
Algorithmic Manipulation (GenAI/Dark Patterns)
       │
       ▼
Cognitive Distortion & Suppression of the Brain’s System 1 (Kahneman, 2011)
       │
       ▼
Defects of Will (Mistake / Fraud / Undue Influence – Art. 1321 Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek))
       │
       ▼
Null and Void / Contract Annulment & Restitution of Rights (Art. 1365 Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek))
```

The diagram illustrates how algorithmic behavioral engineering can be qualified as a novel form of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) or digital fraud (*bedrog*) (Calo, 2014; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). When technology firms deploy predictive algorithms to detect a person’s psychological vulnerabilities—e.g., during periods of financial desperation or chronic loneliness—and then present commercial offers or digital contracts while the victim’s mental resilience is at its nadir, the freedom of will is fundamentally compromised (Zuboff, 2019). Under modern consumer‑protection and contract law principles, such contracts should be rescindable on the basis of Article 1321 Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) in conjunction with Article 1365 Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) because the defect of will stems from information asymmetry and cognitive manipulation (Subekti, 2005).

At the international level, the juridical response to this threat is beginning to take concrete shape through the **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**. Article 5 of the regulation expressly prohibits certain AI practices that pose an “unacceptable risk” (Floridi, 2013). This includes AI systems that employ subliminal techniques beyond a person’s awareness, or that deliberately exploit the vulnerabilities of specific at‑risk groups (such as children or persons with mental disabilities) in a manner that materially harms their behavior to the extent that it is likely to cause significant physical or psychological injury (Hildebrandt, 2015). The prohibition marks a historic milestone: for the first time, positive law explicitly recognises AI‑based cognitive manipulation as a human‑rights violation that must be absolutely barred (Jonas, 1979).

In Indonesia, the **Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)** provides a crucial legal foundation, although implementation challenges remain formidable (Tim Penyusun UU PDP, 2022). The processing of personal data by AI systems for profiling and behavioral engineering must comply with the principle of lawful consent, purpose limitation, and the data subject’s right to object to decisions based solely on automated processing (*automated decision‑making*), including profiling that produces legal effects or significantly impacts the data subject, as guaranteed within contemporary data‑protection frameworks (Farahany, 2023).

Nevertheless, formal rules on paper will never suffice if judges and law‑enforcement agencies fail to grasp the neuro‑psychological dimensions of modern cyber offences (Weizenbaum, 1976). Protecting mental autonomy in the age of artificial intelligence demands a paradigmatic shift: from a passive privacy model—merely safeguarding data against leakage—to an active cognitive‑liberty model that shields the integrity of thought processes and free will from algorithmic exploitation (Zuboff, 2019; Calo, 2014). Without this doctrinal transformation, civil law and digital regulation will remain spectators as human mental autonomy is gradually eroded by invisible lines of code.
